title: What is coordinated omission in load testing? Why does a closed-model tool like JMeter hide tail latency while an open-model tool like wrk2 or k6 exposes the true p99? Explain constant-arrival-rate versus wait-for-response.

s1_definition.profdef: Coordinated omission is a measurement error where a load generator, by waiting for each response before sending the next request, accidentally stops sending requests exactly when the system is slow, so the slow periods are under-sampled and the reported tail latency is far better than reality. A closed-model (wait-for-response) tool like JMeter has a fixed number of virtual users that each send-wait-send, so a stall is counted as one slow sample instead of the hundreds of requests that would have piled up. An open-model (constant-arrival-rate) tool like wrk2 or k6 sends requests on a fixed schedule regardless of responses, so a stall produces many delayed samples and the measured p99 reflects true tail latency including queueing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine measuring how long customers wait at National Bank of India's single teller. In the closed model you have ten "testers" who each walk up, wait however long it takes, get served, then walk back and queue again. If the teller freezes for a minute, those ten testers simply wait patiently — you record ten long waits, nothing more. But in real life, customers keep arriving every few seconds whether or not the teller is frozen, so during that frozen minute a huge line forms and everyone in it waited a long time. The open model keeps "customers arriving on schedule" during the freeze, so it captures the whole backed-up line. Coordinated omission is the closed model politely pausing arrivals during the freeze and then reporting that the bank is fast.
s1_definition.oneliner: Coordinated omission is when your load tool stops sending requests exactly when the server stalls, so closed-model wait-for-response tools hide tail latency while open-model constant-arrival-rate tools expose the true p99.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Coordinated omission is a measurement error where a load generator, by waiting for each response before sending the next request, accidentally stops sending requests exactly when the system is slow, so the slow periods are under-sampled and the reported tail latency is far better than reality. A closed-model (wait-for-response) tool like JMeter has a fixed number of virtual users that each send-wait-send, so a stall is counted as one slow sample instead of the hundreds of requests that would have piled up. An open-model (constant-arrival-rate) tool like wrk2 or k6 sends requests on a fixed schedule regardless of responses, so a stall produces many delayed samples and the measured p99 reflects true tail latency including queueing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine measuring how long customers wait at National Bank of India's single teller. In the closed model you have ten "testers" who each walk up, wait however long it takes, get served, then walk back and queue again. If the teller freezes for a minute, those ten testers simply wait patiently — you record ten long waits, nothing more. But in real life, customers keep arriving every few seconds whether or not the teller is frozen, so during that frozen minute a huge line forms and everyone in it waited a long time. The open model keeps "customers arriving on schedule" during the freeze, so it captures the whole backed-up line. Coordinated omission is the closed model politely pausing arrivals during the freeze and then reporting that the bank is fast.

**One line to remember:** Coordinated omission is when your load tool stops sending requests exactly when the server stalls, so closed-model wait-for-response tools hide tail latency while open-model constant-arrival-rate tools expose the true p99.

sections.s2_technical:
In a closed model, you configure N virtual users. Each user runs a loop: send a request, block until the response arrives, think for a moment, then send the next. The crucial property is that the next request's send time depends on the previous response's arrival time. So if the server stalls for one second, that user simply sends its next request one second later. The stall is coordinated with the measurement — the tool omitted all the requests that a real, independent client population would have sent during that second. This is exactly why the name is coordinated omission. JMeter's default thread-group model and many classic tools behave this way.

The damage is concentrated in the tail. Averages and medians survive reasonably, but p99 and p99.9 collapse to fiction. Suppose your service normally answers in two milliseconds, but once per thousand requests it stalls for one second. In a closed model with, say, one hundred users, that stall produces roughly one hundred samples of about one second and then everyone resumes — so the histogram shows a modest tail. In reality, if requests arrive at ten thousand per second, a one-second stall means about ten thousand requests queued up behind it, each experiencing between zero and one second of extra queueing delay. The true p99 is dominated by that queue, and the closed model never generated those ten thousand delayed requests.

In an open model, the load generator sends requests on a fixed schedule — for example one request every one hundred microseconds for ten thousand per second — independently of when responses come back. This is constant-arrival-rate. If the server stalls, the scheduled requests still "arrive" (the tool records their intended send time), and their latency is measured from the scheduled send time, not from when the tool finally managed to dispatch them. Tools like wrk2, k6 (with a constant-arrival-rate executor), Gatling (with an open injection profile), and Vegeta are built this way. The measured latency therefore includes the queueing that real users would feel.

There is also a correction technique for tools that can only run closed-model: latency correction, sometimes called compensating for coordinated omission. The idea is that if you expected a request every one hundred microseconds but a response took one second, you back-fill the histogram with the synthetic latencies those omitted requests would have had — the first would have waited about one second, the next about one second minus one hundred microseconds, and so on down to near zero. HdrHistogram offers `recordValueWithExpectedInterval(value, expectedInterval)` for exactly this, and wrk2's whole design is built around it. For example `histogram.recordValueWithExpectedInterval(latencyUs, 100)` records the measured latency and synthesises the omitted samples for a one-hundred-microsecond expected interval.

The senior-level nuance is that you must separate throughput from latency. A closed model naturally caps throughput at the system's capacity because users cannot send faster than the system responds, which is useful for finding saturation but useless for honest latency percentiles. An open model lets you fix the arrival rate and then watch latency explode as you approach capacity, which is exactly what you want for an SLO like "p99 under one hundred milliseconds at ten thousand transactions per second". Another nuance: if your open-model tool cannot keep up and its own request scheduler falls behind, you reintroduce coordinated omission on the client side, so you must monitor the generator's own health and run it on a separate, well-provisioned host. A final nuance is that real production traffic is open — users and upstream systems arrive on their own schedule — so the open model is the one that matches reality for a payments API.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is about to launch a new payments confirmation endpoint with an SLO of p99 under one hundred milliseconds at ten thousand transactions per second. The performance team ran JMeter with one hundred threads, saw a p99 of twelve milliseconds, and signed off. On launch day the p99 was over eight hundred milliseconds and customers complained. The post-mortem blamed coordinated omission.

Problem 1 — the service normally responds in two milliseconds but has a periodic garbage-collection pause of about two hundred milliseconds. In the closed JMeter run, when the pause hit, the one hundred threads simply waited and sent their next request late, so only about one hundred requests recorded the pause. This is exactly coordinated omission: the tool stopped generating load during the stall.

Problem 2 — in production, requests arrive from millions of customers on their own schedule at ten thousand per second. During a two-hundred-millisecond pause, about two thousand requests queue up, and each of those waits. The true p99 must include that queueing. This is exactly what an open, constant-arrival-rate model captures.

Problem 3 — we want to prove the difference in numbers, not just words. We simulate a service with a baseline two-millisecond latency and an occasional two-hundred-millisecond stall, then measure it two ways using HdrHistogram: once recording only the measured latency (closed-model style) and once using `recordValueWithExpectedInterval` (open-model correction). The corrected p99 will be dramatically higher, showing the hidden tail.

The code will have a `PaymentService` that simulates baseline latency and periodic stalls, a `ClosedModelHarness` that records only measured latency, an `OpenModelHarness` that uses the expected-interval correction, and a `LoadTestDemo` main class that runs both against the same service and prints the two p99 numbers side by side so the gap is obvious.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build (needs HdrHistogram on the classpath)
mvn clean package

# Run the closed-vs-open comparison
java -cp target/classes:$(cat cp.txt) com.bank.loadtest.LoadTestDemo

# Real open-model tools you would use in CI against the actual endpoint:
# wrk2 at a fixed rate (constant arrival), -R is requests/sec:
wrk2 -t4 -c100 -d60s -R10000 --latency http://localhost:8080/api/v1/payments/confirm

# k6 with a constant-arrival-rate executor:
k6 run --vus 200 --duration 60s payments_open_model.js
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is fifty thousand payment-confirm calls against a service with a two-millisecond baseline and a two-hundred-millisecond stall on every five-hundredth call. The open model expects one request every one hundred microseconds.

Step 1 — the closed harness sends one confirm, waits for it, records the latency, then sends the next. For the four hundred ninety-nine fast calls it records about two milliseconds each. On the five-hundredth call the service stalls two hundred milliseconds, so it records a single two-hundred-millisecond sample and then calmly resumes. The histogram sees roughly one slow sample per five hundred.

Step 2 — the closed harness computes its percentiles. Because only about one in five hundred samples is slow, p99 (the worst one percent) is still dominated by baseline samples, so it reports a small p99, around two to three milliseconds. The tail is hidden.

Step 3 — the open harness sends the same calls but records each with `recordValueWithExpectedInterval(latencyUs, 100)`. For fast calls this behaves normally. But when a call takes two hundred milliseconds while the schedule expected a request every one hundred microseconds, HdrHistogram recognises that about two thousand scheduled requests were omitted during that stall and back-fills them with synthetic latencies descending from two hundred milliseconds down toward zero.

Step 4 — the open harness computes its percentiles over the real plus synthetic samples. Now a large block of high-latency samples exists for every stall, so p99 climbs sharply — toward the stall magnitude — reflecting the queueing real customers would feel.

Step 5 — the demo prints both. The closed median and open median are similar (baseline is unchanged), but the open p99 and p99.9 are far larger than the closed ones. The gap between the two p99 numbers is the coordinated omission that the JMeter sign-off missed.

Step 6 — the lesson is logged: the open p99 is the number customers actually feel, so the SLO must be validated with a constant-arrival-rate tool, not a wait-for-response one.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Coordinated omission is a measurement error in load testing where the load generator stops sending requests exactly when the system is slow, so the slow periods are under-sampled and the reported tail latency looks far better than reality. It happens in a closed model, where a fixed number of virtual users each send a request, wait for the response, then send the next. Because the next send time depends on the previous response, a server stall simply delays the next request — the tool omits all the requests a real, independent client population would have sent during the stall, and that omission is coordinated with the very slowness we are trying to measure. JMeter's default thread-group model behaves this way.

The damage lands entirely in the tail. Medians and averages survive, but p99 and p99.9 become fiction. If a service is normally two milliseconds but stalls for two hundred milliseconds periodically, a closed model records just a handful of slow samples and resumes, so its p99 stays small. In production, requests arrive on their own schedule, so during that same stall thousands of requests queue up and every one of them is slow — that queueing is the real p99.

An open model fixes this by using a constant arrival rate: the generator sends requests on a fixed schedule regardless of when responses come back, and it measures latency from the scheduled send time. So the queueing during a stall is captured honestly. Tools like wrk2, k6 with a constant-arrival-rate executor, Gatling with an open profile, and Vegeta all work this way. For tools stuck in closed mode, HdrHistogram's recordValueWithExpectedInterval back-fills the omitted samples by synthesising the latencies the queued requests would have had, which is exactly how wrk2 is built internally.

In my work this was not theory. At National Bank of India we signed off a payments endpoint on a JMeter p99 of twelve milliseconds, then saw over eight hundred milliseconds on launch day. The culprit was a periodic garbage-collection pause that the closed model hid, because the fixed thread pool just waited through each pause. I re-ran the test with wrk2 at a fixed ten thousand requests per second and the true p99 appeared immediately, which let us tune the collector before the next release. The principle I always state is that production traffic is open — users arrive on their own schedule — so latency SLOs must be validated with a constant-arrival-rate tool, and the generator itself must run on a separate, well-provisioned host so it never becomes the bottleneck and reintroduces coordinated omission on the client side.
